extracted.intended_audience: Navy contract administrators, major/sub-claimants, OPNAV policy staff, and policymakers responsible for commercial activity (CA) implementation and oversight
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for planning, implementing, administering, and assessing Navy commercial activity (contracting-out) studies and post-award contract administration, with emphasis on performance, quality assurance, cost comparison, staffing, and policy guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance assessment methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance assessments were made primarily by using observation (in all cases) and the results of Quality Assurance inspections (in all but one of the cases). Additionally, 56% indicated that performance was evaluated using external inspection results and 78% said customer satisfaction measures were used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists the acceptable/used methods: observation, QA inspections, external inspections, and customer satisfaction measures. The report notes that although formal measurement programs were used frequently, objective pre- and post-award statistics were seldom provided (only three commands), implying evaluators should collect and compare objective performance data to substantiate assessments. Poor database management or control systems may impede objective measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of objective pre- and post-award performance data
rubrics_metrics.description: Only three commands provided performance statistics comparing pre-award and post-award performance; examination showed slight/no significant declines or no change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/implication: objective, comparative statistics are important to substantiate 'satisfactory' performance claims; lack of such data indicates need for better control systems and database management to monitor performance objectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductions for substandard performance / deduction clause
rubrics_metrics.description: A majority (56%) of the commands had taken deductions for substandard performance despite acceptable performance overall; some contracts initially lacked a deduction clause although current contracts included one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical notes: deductions taken were generally less than 1% of contract price; commands also issued Contract Discrepancy Reports in support of deductions. Absence of a deduction clause can prevent enforcement and may lead to tolerating poor performance. Record deductions with supporting documentation (QAE reports) to justify enforcement and litigation positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation and Contract Discrepancy Reports (CDRs) to support enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Four commands indicated they had issued Contract Discrepancy Reports both in addition to and in support of deductions. Poorly documented QA evaluations can seriously undermine enforcement of standards and jeopardize litigation positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes the anti-pattern: inadequate documentation by Quality Assurance Evaluators undermines government's ability to assess deductions and enforce contract standards. QA reports and other substantiating documentation should be assembled (used in one litigation example of ~20 documents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractor prior experience / qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: All respondents indicated that the current contractor was experienced in the type of operation they were performing, with approximately 67% having performed similar work for the Navy or Department of Defense previously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractor experience—especially prior DoD/Navy experience—is an important evaluative factor when predicting successful performance and transition outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procurement method and solicitation content (sealed bid, negotiated procurement, technical proposals, set-asides)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two respondents used sealed bids, two used Small Business Set-aside procedures, majority used negotiated procurement. Technical proposals were used in a majority (56%) of awards; some commands were not involved in the pre-award survey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-award survey defined as an on-site visit to assess financial integrity and technical competence. Guidance implies selecting appropriate procurement method, including technical proposals and conducting pre-award surveys to vet contractors is important for successful outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-award survey (financial and technical assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pre-award survey is an on-site visit to the prospective contractor's facilities to assess both the financial integrity and technical competence of the company and its personnel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pre-award surveys as a metric to assess contractor viability; lack of command involvement in pre-award surveys may increase transition risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of the cost comparison process
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents were asked 'Do you feel that the cost comparison process accurately reflects the cost of contracting out?' Only two responded positively; many felt the cost comparison underestimated actual costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified undercounted costs include contract administration staffing, negotiation time, QA vehicle costs, loss of productivity due to morale, and post-award litigation. Cost comparisons should account for front-end transition costs, ongoing admin/QA costs, morale/productivity impacts, and likely litigation or contingency expenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for morale and productivity impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Loss of productivity on the part of remaining government employees (due to morale/anxiety over job loss) is not accounted for in the cost comparison process and respondents felt such impacts affected productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should include indirect costs from morale and staff displacement when estimating costs of contracting out; omission can lead to underestimation of true costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of litigation/post-award costs in cost estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents noted that post-award litigation costs are not accounted for; while only two had litigation on current contracts, aggregate costs could be significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include expected litigation/claims handling costs (time and money assembling litigation packages) when evaluating contracting-out costs; at minimum collect documentation to reduce litigation risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate contract administration and QA staffing
rubrics_metrics.description: All respondents indicated that an adequate and competent contract administration staff was critical to contract success. The report notes the Cost Comparison Handbook staffing allowances were inadequate for complex/multi-function contracts; one claimant recommended ~18-20 people headed by a Service Contract Manager for multi-function contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staffing should be tailored to contract complexity; centralized claimant negotiation for additional QA staffing may be necessary. Adequate staffing ensures deficient performance is documented and corrected and reduces costly reprocurement/resolicitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed and complete Quality Assurance (QA) Plan
rubrics_metrics.description: A detailed and complete Quality Assurance Plan in conjunction with a competent QA staff can ensure that deficient performance is documented and corrected. Four of nine contracted CAs had never implemented a QA plan; another delayed implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement QA plans promptly (not 16 months after start). QA plans should include sampling and QA techniques (NAVFAC manual cited as an example). Proper QA helps document deficiencies, support deductions, and avoid more costly measures like termination/resolicitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized claimant guidance and implementation teams
rubrics_metrics.description: Under extensive pre-award and post-award guidance from COMNAVAIRPAC, CINCPACFLT activities experienced relatively short transition periods and only minor deficiencies. Centralized claimant involvement and implementation teams provide oversight, lessons learned, and technical assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: decentralized claimancy with minimal staff led to repeated mistakes and more costly remedial actions. Recommendation: use centralized claimant teams to provide oversight, share lessons learned, and assist with management study, MEO, and PWS development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and completeness of the Performance Work Statement (PWS)
rubrics_metrics.description: A vaguely written, unenforceable PWS contributed to contractor failure; PWS inadequacies were a primary cause of claims and poor performance. Defining performance requirements is complex and changes over time, especially in complex operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PWS must be clear, enforceable, and anticipate workload, technology, and mission changes where possible. Poorly written PWSs can lead to inability to enforce standards, inappropriate reimbursement structures, claims, and costly resolicitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailoring contract type to operation complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: The type of contract should be tailored to the complexity of the operation and need for coordination: multi-function/umbrella contracts for high coordination, single-function contracts for stand-alone operations. Many respondents preferred Cost Plus Award Fee for complex operations and Firm Fixed Price for less complex ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: deduction clauses are negative incentives and litigable, increasing documentation requirements; award fees are positive incentives and not litigable, reducing documentation burden. Firm Fixed Price minimizes inflated contractor costs for simpler operations. Select contract type to balance incentives and administrative burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting limited early substandard performance during transition
rubrics_metrics.description: Several respondents allowed a small amount of substandard performance in early stages of the contract without assessing deductions to enhance working relations and allow a normal learning curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice: tolerate minor deficiencies during initial transition, but ensure that after the period an adequate QA/admin staff enforces standards. This balances relationship-building with eventual enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for post-award policy/guidance (default, bankruptcy, sustaining operations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many sample activities indicated the need for general guidelines for dealing with contractor default or bankruptcy and sustaining service operations in the event of contract termination; the report recommends OPNAV-443 issue instruction on sustaining operations post-termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare front-end plans for post-decision activities, including contingency options, temporary staffing procedures, and instructions for sustaining operations when a contractor fails. This reduces disruption and ad-hoc costly measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-end planning for post-decision activities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Government needs to devote more front-end planning to post-decision activities; the process does not end with the cost comparison. If contracted, the activity must have a plan for contract administration and QA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improved front-end planning reduces back-end problems; include contract administration, QA, contingency plans, and anticipated admin costs in initial studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and consistency of fringe benefit/acceleration rates in cost estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconsistencies noted between rates used in budget formulation (16-17%) and those used in cost comparison (in excess of 27%), with historical fluctuations, highlight concern over accuracy of government labor cost estimates in cost comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consistent and realistic fringe benefit and escalation/acceleration rates when estimating government labor costs in cost comparison studies to avoid distorted comparisons.
